newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt says Camp David won't solve peace problems.
newsitem.headline: Egypt says Camp David won't solve peace problems.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said on Monday a proposal by Israel to hold U.S.-led negotiations like those at Camp David in 1978 would not solve the problems of the Israeli-Palestinian peace process.
But Mubarak welcomed a U.S. initiative for a temporary freeze on the building of Jewish settlements while Israeli and Palestinian officials hold peace talks.

U.S. President Bill Clinton and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu were due to hold talks in Washington on Monday to discuss new ideas that U.S. officials hope will defuse tensions over new Jewish settlements in Arab East Jerusalem.
"Camp David will not solve the problems now," Mubarak told reporters after he cast his vote in local council elections.

Egypt became the first Arab state to sign a peace treaty with Israel in 1979 after then U.S. president Jimmy Carter hosted intensive three-way peace talks with Egyptian and Israeli leaders at the U.S. presidential retreat at Camp David.

During the Camp David negotiations, Carter often met separately with Israeli prime minister Menachem Begin and Egyptian president Anwar Sadat -- pressuring each one to move closer to the position of the other.

Netanyahu has proposed that he and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat reach a final peace agreement within six months -- and said the goal might require Camp David-like talks to break the current impasse.
U.S. Vice President Al Gore said on Sunday that Clinton was not receptive to Netanyahu's suggestion.

Israel's decision to break ground at the Jerusalem settlement site last month brought the peace talks to near collapse and prompted Arab League foreign ministers meeting in Cairo to recommend that Arab states backtrack on normal relations with Israel.
Mubarak was positive about a U.S. intitiative to temporarily halt Jewish settlement building while Palestinians and Israelis sort out their differences.
"If they (U.S. officials) could manage to make Mr Netanyahu agree to it, it will be a very good step forward. It will help us push the peace process forward and support it," Mubarak said.
"Let them halt the settlements for the time being and in the negotiations all the problems will be solved," he added.
Netanyahu was adamant ahead of his U.S. visit that he would not scrap the settlement at Jebel Abu Ghneim, which is also known as Har Homa.
Palestinians have clashed with Israeli soldiers in the West Bank almost every day since Israel broke ground to build a 6,500-unit housing project on land captured during the 1967 Middle East war.

Arafat said in New Delhi on Monday that Israel had declared war against the Middle East peace process, and urged members of the Non-Aligned Movement to review their diplomatic ties with the Jewish state.
Mubarak said it was better for Egypt not to sever its ties with Israel so that Cairo could continue in its role as unofficial sponsor of the peace talks.
"If we cut our diplomatic relations or do anything like that it will mean we will not be able to contact the other side to help solve the existing problem," Mubarak said.

Egypt, Jordan and the Palestinians, who already have peace agreements with Israel, are not required to enforce the Arab League recommendation to backtrack on normalisation with Israel, restore the economic boycott and withdraw from multilateral peace talks.
